title: U.S. strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island; Iran retaliates with ballistic missiles at Jordan bases (August 30, 2026)
dek: U.S. forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on August 30, the first known American attack on Iran since late July. Iran responded by launching ballistic missiles at U.S. bases in Jordan. The exchange marks a resumption of tit-for-tat military action six months into the undeclared war.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: U.S. military struck Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on August 30, 2026, after observing IRGC forces preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz; Iran retaliated with ballistic missiles at U.S. bases in Jordan.
bottom_line: The pause in direct military action lasted exactly one month. The resumed strikes and counter-strikes occur with the Strait of Hormuz still operating below normal capacity and no reported diplomatic negotiations. The August 30 exchange shows both sides preparing for sustained engagement rather than seeking off-ramps.
body: U.S. forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on August 30, according to BBC News reporting. The strike marked the first known American attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July. U.S. Central Command spokesman Commander Tim Hawkins said IRGC forces had been observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the strike killed and wounded several people; the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency reported two people killed and two others injured.

The strike resumed direct military action after a month without major escalation in a conflict now six months old. The U.S. and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, triggering Iranian counterattacks on Israel, U.S. bases, and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. Global oil prices have risen approximately 30 percent compared to pre-war levels, according to CBS News reporting.

Iran responded to the August 30 strike by attacking U.S. bases in Jordan with ballistic missiles. The IRGC said it had targeted the King Hussein and al-Azraq bases and claimed to have caused heavy damage to technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and fighter jet positions. Jordan's armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that breached the kingdom's airspace at dawn on Monday, per BBC News reporting.

The conflict has severely disrupted global shipping through a waterway that carries roughly 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas. Roughly 120 oil tankers transited the strait daily before the war began, according to CBS News. Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, said the military had cleared mines laid by the IRGC and enabled nearly 1,500 commercial vessels to transit the strait under coordinated protection over the past several months, moving 750 million barrels of crude oil out of the Persian Gulf. Iran has exported zero barrels of oil from its shores since the U.S. resumed a naval blockade in mid-July, Cooper said.

Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad acknowledged Thursday that the country's exports had declined but said oil continued to move to customers via distant waters despite the blockade. Iran is currently forcing tanker traffic to pass by Larak Island for inspection and reportedly demanding $2 million per vessel to cross, per BBC News reporting.

Larak Island sits directly on the Strait of Hormuz just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas. IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi called the U.S. strike a strategic miscalculation and said the enemy would face consequences in economic and military fields. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi rejected President Trump's claims about mine clearance as propaganda deception. Some U.S. allies reportedly do not believe the strait has been fully de-mined, according to Bloomberg reporting cited by CBS News.

Iran faces renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on August 24 aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies. Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the sanctions as evidence of U.S. military failure rather than legitimate economic measures.
